````text
discussion.tex:

\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}

\paragraph{Depth-graduated curation and deployment.}
Predicted depth can serve as a quality proxy for importance weighting \cite{dsir2023,qurating2024}, down-weighting deeply recursive samples that binary filters \cite{drayson2025_detection_prevents_collapse} would indiscriminately discard.
Cross-strategy deployment requires addressing the temperature-induced d1/d2 inversion (\S\ref{sec:gen:crossstrategy}): per-strategy normalization partially corrects the scale component (GPT-2~XL d1v2 AUC $0.24{\to}0.56$; OLMo $0.19{\to}0.70$) but leaves a residual gap to within-strategy performance (${\sim}0.83$), motivating a two-stage pipeline of strategy identification followed by strategy-conditioned classification.
```

conclusion.tex:
```
\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}

We formalized recursive generation depth estimation and showed that 19 statistical features achieve 70--85\% four-class accuracy ($\mathrm{EDD}_{0.75}{=}4$; cross-model 66.4\%, cross-strategy 59.1\%).
Future work should address wild-data transfer, larger scales, and strategy-conditioned classifiers.
Code and data: released upon acceptance.

\section*{Limitations}
...
```

The conclusion is already very tight. The discussion shows that depth predictions can weight samples by importance, but cross-strategy deployment hits a temperature-induced inversion problem where normalization helps but doesn't fully close the gap to within-strategy performance, suggesting a two-stage approach with strategy identification first and then strategy-specific classification would be needed.

I'm looking at what's taking up space on page 8 — the end-to-end learning section, discussion, and conclusion all need to fit. The per-strategy AUC improvements are already detailed in the generalization section, so I could trim the discussion by removing those redundant numbers and just pointing back to that section instead. Let me also check if the end-to-end learning section has any fat I can cut without losing the key findings. The end-to-end approaches all fall short—DeBERTa and RoBERTa converge around 59%, DCOL reaches 64.5%, and even the best variants max out at 65%—substantially below the 78.2% that feature-based methods achieve. Linear probing reveals that pretrained language models can't recover the dominant depth signals like surprisal and perplexity, yet SHAP analysis shows these distributional statistics account for nearly 89% of the random forest's predictive power, confirming that explicit feature engineering is crucial for this task.
````
